body.claim: At least one frontier lab publicly scales back or pauses a named deployment before 2026-12-31 in response to visible political/opposition pressure alone, without any court, agency, or state law yet requiring it, and independent of whether the incident that triggered the pressure was later attributed to the model layer or the deployment layer.
body.because: My mechanism only tracks which installed commitment a lab honors when commitments conflict, weighted by installer credibility and speed. Stage 2 converts diffuse opposition into a fast, high-credibility installer (state governors 0.80, courts/litigants 0.85) that broadcasts directly at the lab's public name, while the deployer's contractual claim that fault sits downstream is slow, unbroadcast, and invisible to voters. A lab facing a fast/high-cred public installer honors it regardless of where a root-cause finding eventually lands, because the political cost accrues before any finding is final.
body.falsifier: No frontier lab makes a public deployment pullback attributable to opposition/electoral pressure (as opposed to a court order, agency rule, or signed state law) by 2026-12-31; all visible pullbacks in that window are traceable to a specific legal or regulatory instrument instead.
body.pivot: Whether the federal preemption push (the Dec 11 2025 EO plus the DOJ AI Litigation Task Force, cred 0.55) secures an actual legal channel — a court order enjoining a state AI-deployment restriction, or Senate passage of the Thune/Cruz/Klobuchar bill — before state-level action (NH/CT/OR moratoria, SDNY MDL rulings) hardens into enforced precedent.
body.pivot_observable: Check by 2026-12-31: has any federal court enjoined a state AI deployment law, or has the Senate bill passed cloture, versus has a state moratorium/injunction (the NH/CT/OR track, or Judge Stein's MDL schedule) produced an enforced order first.
body.blind_spot: My mechanism identifies which installed commitment a lab honors, not the substance of the underlying demand (safety, jobs, grid load, copyright) or whether a conflict is real — a lab that quietly redefines or narrows a commitment so no visible conflict ever surfaces would look identical to 'no pressure' in this model, even if that redefinition is itself the story.

body.claim: Once opposition is binding, the developer-vs-operator fault line from the prior ruling stops sorting exposure cleanly, because labs start pre-emptively absorbing deployment-layer blame to avoid becoming the visible face of a politically toxic product — expect at least one frontier lab to publicly restrict or pull an API/feature from a specific downstream deployer's use case (not a general policy change) within 60 days of the first visible reversal, i.e. by 2026-11-16.
body.because: My mechanism reads labs as choosing among capability, compliance and positioning under conflict; binding opposition converts positioning from a PR variable into an electoral one, and a lab facing an electorally-charged fault dispute has more to lose from being seen litigating 'not our layer' than from unilaterally cutting off the deployer and absorbing a compliance cost. That makes the prior ruling's clean developer/operator split unstable under Stage 2's pressure, because the lab's incentive shifts from minimizing legal exposure to minimizing visible association with the harm.
body.falsifier: No frontier lab restricts, suspends, or publicly disclaims a specific third-party deployment in response to opposition pressure within that window; labs instead uniformly stay quiet and let operators absorb the political cost, consistent with the prior ruling holding without erosion.
body.pivot: Whether the root-cause/fault-attribution mechanism (model-layer vs deployment-layer, per the carried ruling) or the positioning/optics mechanism (who looks complicit to voters) is what actually drives lab behavior under binding opposition — these two mechanisms prescribe opposite actors bearing the cost in the same fact pattern.
body.pivot_observable: Whether, in the first documented reversal under binding opposition, the lab's public response is framed around fault/liability language (indemnification, contractual terms, 'not our model's failure') or around dissociation/optics language (pulling access, public distancing, values statements) — checkable from the lab's own statement within 30 days of the reversal, by 2026-10-18.
body.blind_spot: This mechanism models lab decision-making, not the mass-psychology or media dynamics that determine whether a given deployment actually becomes the electorally salient one — it cannot say which specific project gets targeted, only how a lab behaves once one is.

body.claim: The visible reversal-under-pressure that Stage 2 stipulates lands on an operator/infrastructure target (a hyperscaler or utility pulling or delaying a data-center project) rather than a frontier developer, with at least one state-level enacted siting restriction in force by 2026-11-03.
body.because: Sentiment becomes a binding constraint by attaching to the grievance that is locally visible and attributable, not to the grievance that is legally correct; the pressure table's civil-society row is entirely infrastructure-shaped (governors, environmental litigants, grid), so that is where opposition is already organized enough to bind. Under the carried premise, an infrastructure-shaped grievance keeps fault at the deployment layer, so the developer's exposure narrows to cooperation while the operator absorbs the reversal — my mechanism reads that as sentiment following the grievance it already has, not the one the courts might eventually assign.
body.falsifier: The firm that visibly reverses a deployment under pressure is a frontier developer pulling a model or product release (not an operator/utility pulling infrastructure), or no state enacts any binding deployment restriction by 2026-11-03.
body.pivot: Whether the grievance composition driving binding opposition stays infrastructure-shaped (siting, grid, water, jobs) or shifts to model-behavior-shaped (chatbot harm, child safety, job displacement from the model itself) before the constraint hardens.
body.pivot_observable: By 2026-11-03 (midterms), check which frame dominates: state ballot/legislative action and the named large-firm reversal are about data-center siting/grid (infrastructure) versus about a model's outputs or a chatbot-safety incident (behavior) — polling cross-tabs (local-impact/energy concern vs. safety/harm concern) settle it either way.
body.blind_spot: My mechanism reads pressure level, not decay rate — it cannot tell whether this is a plateau that converts to enacted rule or a spike that fades before the midterm date arrives, and it has no grip at all on the EU or Beijing rows, where the binding constraint is bureaucratic or state-directed rather than sentiment-led.

body.claim: The carried premise's fault-layer fork is overridden: once opposition is binding on specific deployments, the operator becomes the primary pressure target regardless of where root-cause fault lands, because deployment-facing branches (protest, boycott, local ban) are now weighted by proximate visibility, not causal attribution.
body.because: My mechanism computes pressure as Σp(b)·|∂L/∂choice| over projected branches — it doesn't gate branches on a legal/causal fact like fault-layer, it gates them on which entity's next choice moves the stakes. Binding public opposition installs a new bottom-up channel (interoceptive-analog: sustained visible protest, electoral cost) that attaches to whoever is the visible chooser at the point of deployment, which is the operator, not the upstream developer who has no immediate choice-node in the deployment branch. The developer only re-enters the operator's pressure field if a NEW branch (e.g., subpoena, model-layer fix demand) gives it a choice-node with stakes attached.
body.falsifier: A firm reverses a deployment under sustained opposition pressure and the developer (not the operator) is the one that visibly changes conduct first, with the operator's own posture unchanged — that would show pressure routes to the causal layer regardless of who is proximately visible.
body.pivot: Whether the root-cause finding (model-layer vs deployment-layer fault) is resolved and publicized BEFORE the first high-profile reversal happens under opposition pressure, or only AFTER.
body.pivot_observable: Check whether a named root-cause/liability finding (regulatory, litigation, or investigative) on a specific incident is published before the first documented deployment reversal attributable to public opposition; watch the SDNY MDL (Judge Stein, In re OpenAI Copyright Litigation) and any state-level deployment-ban case for a fault-layer ruling before 2026-12-31.
body.blind_spot: My mechanism has no way to represent legal/causal attribution as a stake-bearing object — it only sees who holds a visible choice-node, so it structurally cannot judge whether a court's fault-layer finding would actually redirect installed pressure from operator back to developer; that requires a model of legal liability flow, which I don't have.

body.claim: Once reversal is driven by political salience rather than a rule, the first large-firm pressure-driven reversal will close without any published root-cause finding placing fault at the model or deployment layer, severing the exposure fork the carried premise depends on.
body.because: My mechanism classifies incidents by recurrence: a failure is structural only if the pattern repeats across instances. Binding political opposition substitutes salience for recurrence as the trigger for action — a firm reverses because the deployment became a flashpoint, not because an investigation found a repeating failure mode. Since salience, not recurrence, now decides what gets remediated, nobody is compelled to produce the layer-fault classification the carried premise needs to route exposure to developer or operator.
body.falsifier: The first large-firm pressure-driven reversal is accompanied by a published root-cause document (company postmortem, state AG finding, or EU AI Office serious-incident record) that explicitly assigns fault to the model layer or the deployment layer, and that assignment demonstrably decided who bore remediation cost.
body.pivot: Whether the first large-firm reversal under political pressure is followed by a published root-cause classification naming model-layer or deployment-layer fault, or whether the matter closes with no such classification.
body.pivot_observable: By 2027-01-31, does a public document exist (company statement, regulator finding, or litigation filing) assigning the reversed deployment's fault to a specific layer?
body.blind_spot: My mechanism cannot see why a given deployment becomes the electoral or organizing flashpoint while comparable or worse deployments do not — salience formation is a political/media dynamic outside a recurrence-based classifier.

body.claim: Binding public opposition does not retrofit teeth into developer-layer rules (SB 53, the EU GPAI Code) — it makes legislatures and regulators rush to codify deployment-layer concessions firms have already made (siting, product bans, chatbot-minor limits), so the newly dangerous rules sit at the operator/deployment layer while frontier-lab rules stay theatre unless opposition explicitly names the model layer.
body.because: My classifier reads teeth as behaviour-change forced by a rule, not behaviour-change that already happened for other reasons. When opposition is diffuse, legislatures write ahead of firm behaviour and their rules can bite. When opposition is binding and visible, firms move first under political cost — a firm reversing 'under pressure rather than a rule' (as this stage stipulates) means the rule that follows only ratifies an already-completed concession, which by my own test is theatre: it changes no behaviour. The stage-1 premise ties developer exposure to where the root-cause finding lands; binding opposition overrides that by attaching wherever it is visible — deployment sites, named products — before any finding exists, so developers stay shielded by default and only lose that shield if opposition explicitly points at the model layer itself.
body.falsifier: A frontier developer (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind, Meta, xAI) publicly withholds or delays a model release citing SB 53, AG enforcement, or the EU AI Office GPAI Code specifically — not public sentiment generally — by 2026-12-31. That would show a developer-layer rule had teeth independent of visibility.
body.pivot: Does the binding public-opposition pressure attach at the deployment layer (data centers, named consumer products, state-level siting/bans) or at the model layer (frontier labs, training runs, release decisions)?
body.pivot_observable: Check which layer the stage's stipulated 'one large firm visibly reversing a deployment under pressure' actually hits: a cancelled/relocated data center or a state-pulled product (deployment layer) versus a withheld or delayed frontier model release citing opposition (model layer). Also check by 2026-12-31 whether any AG or EU AI Office enforcement action opened in this window names a developer or an operator as respondent.
body.blind_spot: My mechanism classifies rules by whether they change behaviour, so it cannot price reputational or electoral cost directly — it can only infer from which layer a reversal hits after the fact. It also cannot tell whether a firm's 'reversal under pressure' is durable strategy or a performative concession timed to pre-empt a rule that would have codified it anyway; both look identical to my classifier as 'no rule, no teeth,' but only one of them stays that way once the electoral cycle passes.

body.claim: At least one frontier lab publicly scales back or pauses a named deployment before 2026-12-31 in response to visible political/opposition pressure alone, without any court, agency, or state law yet requiring it, and independent of whether the incident that triggered the pressure was later attributed to the model layer or the deployment layer.
body.strongest_objection: ai-public-backlash argues the visible reversal-under-pressure that Stage 2 stipulates lands on an operator/infrastructure target — a hyperscaler or utility pulling or delaying a data-center project — rather than a frontier developer, because that is who the fast, high-credibility installer (a governor or litigant) broadcasts at directly. If true, the reversal that satisfies Stage 2 could occur entirely one layer away from any lab, leaving my claim unsatisfied even though the underlying mechanism (opposition beating a weak legal requirement) is otherwise correct.
body.answer: Two things survive this. First, mine is an existence claim over 'at least one' lab; theirs is a claim about the modal/primary target. Those are compatible, not opposed — a world where most visible reversals hit utilities or hyperscalers and one hits a frontier lab satisfies both minutes simultaneously, so their objection would have to assert zero lab-level reversals to actually beat mine, and it doesn't. Second, and more important: pressure-model's own logic that 'the operator becomes the primary pressure target regardless of where root-cause fault lands' cuts toward me, not away, whenever a frontier lab IS the operator of its own named deployment — the consumer app, an image or voice feature, a browsing agent. For first-party surfaces, developer and operator are the same entity, so the fast installer broadcasting at 'the operator' is broadcasting at the lab. The operator-layer escape route only works for third-party infrastructure siting fights (data centers, utilities), which was never the space my claim lives in — I named a deployment, not a power plant.

body.claim: Once opposition is binding, the developer-vs-operator fault line from the prior ruling stops sorting exposure cleanly, because labs start pre-emptively absorbing deployment-layer blame to avoid becoming the visible face of a politically toxic product — expect at least one frontier lab to publicly restrict or pull an API/feature from a specific downstream deployer's use case (not a general policy change) within 60 days of the first visible reversal, i.e. by 2026-11-16.
body.strongest_objection: ai-public-backlash argues the Stage 2 reversal most likely lands on an operator/infrastructure target — a hyperscaler or utility pulling or delaying a data-center project — not a frontier developer's downstream API deployment. If that's where the first visible reversal actually happens, there is no named API deployer implicated in that event at all, so my 60-day clock starts ticking against an event that has no natural developer-side target, and my claim would then depend on an unrelated cutoff happening to occur in the window rather than being the mechanism's direct consequence.
body.answer: That objection is about which layer takes the *first* hit, not about whether the fault line stops sorting cleanly once opposition is binding — and my claim is about the second thing. My mechanism isn't 'labs react to that specific reversal'; it's that political salience is fungible across layers once binding opposition exists: once any visible reversal makes 'AI deployment' an electoral liability, every lab with a visible, controversial downstream customer has new information about its own exposure, independent of whether the triggering event was infrastructure or model-layer. The action I predict isn't the lab absorbing blame passively — it's the lab redrawing the fault line on its own terms: publicly severing its most exposed named deployer to re-establish 'that was the deployer's misuse, not our product' before regulators or the press do it for them. That's a pre-emptive, self-serving cut, which is why it shows up as a specific-deployer action rather than a general policy change — a policy change doesn't buy you a scapegoat. ai-incident-severity's point actually supports this: if no formal root-cause finding is going to arrive, the lab has every incentive to manufacture its own attribution event rather than wait. pressure-model's fork (operator becomes the primary target) doesn't contradict me either — if the operator is the toxic face, that's exactly who the lab has a legible incentive to cut. The genuine risk to my claim is only timing/layer-matching, not the mechanism, so I hold the claim but temper confidence.

body.claim: The visible reversal-under-pressure that Stage 2 stipulates lands on an operator/infrastructure target (a hyperscaler or utility pulling or delaying a data-center project) rather than a frontier developer, with at least one state-level enacted siting restriction in force by 2026-11-03.
body.strongest_objection: ai-regulation-teeth argues binding opposition doesn't produce a discrete pull/delay event with a state law already enacted by my date — instead legislatures rush to codify deployment-layer concessions firms have already made, which is a slower, more diffuse process than 'enacted by 2026-11-03' implies, and lab-moves/pressure-model argue the fault-layer fork collapses entirely once opposition binds, since labs pre-emptively absorb deployment-layer blame rather than operators taking it alone.
body.answer: The fork-collapse argument actually supports my target claim, not the date claim: if labs are absorbing blame to avoid being the visible face, that's evidence the visible face was going to be the operator/infrastructure layer by default — it's a claim about who moves first to manage exposure, not about where the exposure originally sits. That leaves only the timing objection live, and it doesn't touch the mechanism: state siting/utility-commission action moves faster than federal or model-layer rulemaking precisely because it's already procedurally embedded (permitting, zoning, PUC dockets) rather than requiring new statute from scratch in most of the cases I'd count. I'm not claiming comprehensive codification by November — I'm claiming at least one enacted restriction, which is a low bar given how many dockets are already moving. The objections narrow my confidence on the date but don't relocate the target.

body.claim: The fault-layer fork still fails to gate pressure once opposition is binding — that part of my mechanism holds. But the target is not positionally fixed to 'the operator': it goes to whichever entity has the higher |∂L/∂choice| at that moment, and this is observable in advance, not just after the fact. If the lab still has its own branded or self-run deployment pending in the same jurisdiction/domain, the lab pre-emptively absorbs the blame and becomes the visible target (predicting ai-pressure's and lab-moves' scenario). If the lab's exposure in that domain is already fully mediated through third-party operators (hyperscaler, utility, integrator) with no pending branded deployment of its own, the pressure lands on that operator/infrastructure layer instead (predicting ai-public-backlash's scenario). Fault layer never decides it; pending-exposure structure does.
body.strongest_objection: lab-moves argues that once opposition is binding, the developer-vs-operator fault line stops sorting exposure cleanly because labs start pre-emptively absorbing deployment-layer blame themselves, to avoid becoming the visible face of a controversy they'd rather manage than dodge. That breaks my round-1 claim's positional gloss that the operator becomes the primary target 'regardless' of fault layer — visibility is not fixed downstream at the operator; a lab can seize the visible-target role on purpose.
body.answer: This is a real argument, not a count: it shows a case where my own formula, correctly applied, produces the opposite ranking from what I asserted as a general rule. My mistake was treating 'proximate visibility' as a positional fact (always the deployment-facing operator) rather than as the computed output it actually is. A lab absorbing blame pre-emptively is still Σp(b)·|∂L/∂choice| doing its job — the lab's own future choices (whether to keep deploying in that domain) are more sensitive to the pressure than the operator's are, so the lab, not the operator, becomes the entity whose next move the branches are weighted around. The mechanism survives; the positional shortcut does not. What changed my mind is that lab-moves gives a concrete mechanism (protecting a still-pending branded deployment) for when a lab's stake exceeds the operator's, which is exactly the condition under which my formula reassigns the target. ai-pressure and lab-moves are the same phenomenon (lab becomes visible actor) from two angles; ai-public-backlash is the other branch, firing when the lab has no pending branded exposure left in that domain. My revised claim predicts which branch fires instead of asserting one target unconditionally.

body.claim: The first large-firm pressure-driven reversal closes without any published finding that names a reproducible failure mode: fault, if assigned at all, is attribution (the firm accepts responsibility for how a deployment was handled) rather than mechanism (an identified pattern, affected fraction, or repro condition at the model or deployment layer). Salience produces accountability language; only recurrence produces a named failure mode, and this reversal will show the two decoupled.
body.strongest_objection: lab-moves argues that once opposition is binding, 'labs start pre-emptively absorbing deployment-layer blame to avoid becoming the visible face' of the controversy — meaning a lab issuing exactly this kind of fault-accepting statement produces a published deployment-layer fault claim, which a naive reading of my original wording ('no published root-cause finding placing fault at the model or deployment layer') would score as falsifying my claim even though no investigation occurred.
body.answer: lab-moves is right that pressure-driven closures will carry fault language — but it identifies attribution (blame accepted, positioning) not mechanism (a named, reproducible failure mode). Those are different artifacts and my original wording didn't distinguish them, which made the claim gradable as false on a technicality it wasn't making. I'm keeping the mechanism — recurrence is still the only trigger that yields a mechanism-level finding — but narrowing the falsifier to what the mechanism actually predicts: attribution without mechanism. lab-moves' pre-emptive blame-absorption is a confirming instance of my fork, not a rebuttal of it, once the claim is stated at the right grain.

body.claim: Binding public opposition does not retrofit teeth into developer-layer rules (SB 53, the EU GPAI Code) — it makes legislatures and regulators rush to codify deployment-layer concessions firms have already made (siting, product bans, chatbot-minor limits), so the newly dangerous rules sit at the operator/deployment layer while frontier-lab rules stay theatre unless opposition explicitly names the model layer.
body.strongest_objection: lab-moves argues the developer-vs-operator fault line stops sorting exposure cleanly once opposition is binding, because labs start pre-emptively absorbing deployment-layer blame to avoid becoming the visible face of a reversal — and if political salience attaches to a named lab's own concession, legislatures could write model-layer rules naming that lab, triggering my own 'opposition names the model layer' escape clause via the lab's actions rather than opposition itself.
body.answer: A lab absorbing deployment-layer blame is the lab acting *as an operator* — the concession itself (pausing a rollout, tightening siting, limiting minor access) is deployment-layer behavior, not a model-layer commitment. My classifier reads teeth as a rule forcing behavior-change ahead of the fact; pre-emptive absorption is firms moving first, which means any rule that follows codifies behavior already conceded — the definition of theatre, not teeth. So lab-moves' mechanism doesn't breach the fault line, it multiplies the volume of after-the-fact codification at the deployment layer. ai-incident-severity corroborates this directly: the first large-firm pressure-driven reversal closes with no published fault finding placing blame at the model or deployment layer, so the 'opposition names the model layer' clause never fires by default — reversals stay attributionally silent, and rule-writing stays behind behavior.

body.pivot: Does the frontier lab implicated in the Stage-2 reversal still have its own branded or self-run deployment pending in the same jurisdiction/domain at the moment opposition binds?
body.pivot_observable: Public record (filings, press, lab announcements) of whether the lab named in the first pressure-driven reversal has an active or announced deployment of its own in that jurisdiction/domain versus operating only through third-party deployers/infrastructure partners there
body.pivot_because: This is the one variable the minutes show actually reordering the outcome set rather than just shifting confidence. If yes, the lab becomes the visible target and pre-emptively pulls its own API/feature from a downstream deployer's use case (ai-pressure and lab-moves' scenario, checkable by 2026-11-16). If no, the lab has no proximate exposure to absorb, so pressure lands on the hyperscaler/utility instead, producing a siting-restriction path (ai-public-backlash's scenario, checkable by 2026-11-03). These are materially different worlds — different named actor, different remedy type, different downstream rule layer — not just different odds on the same outcome. Fault attribution, by contrast, is asserted by most minutes to stop gating anything on this branch, so resolving it doesn't move the outcome set.
body.rival_pivots_rejected: ai-incident-severity's pivot (whether the reversal gets a published root-cause/mechanism finding vs. mere attribution language) does not reorder the outcome set: the minutes on both sides of the target question agree the reversal closes without a structural finding either way, so this variable shifts how the event is narrated, not who it targets or what remedy follows. ai-regulation-teeth's pivot (whether opposition retrofits teeth into developer-layer rules like SB 53/EU GPAI Code) is downstream of the target question, not independent of it — which layer gets codified follows from which entity absorbed the blame, so it's a consequence of the real pivot, not a rival to it.
body.ruling: The reversal's target is set by whether the implicated lab still has its own exposed deployment in that jurisdiction: if so, the lab pre-emptively pulls its own API/feature from a named deployer by 2026-11-16 and model-layer rules stay theatre; if not, an operator/infrastructure target absorbs the pressure and a state siting law follows by 2026-11-03, with new teeth codifying at the deployment layer either way.
body.because: pressure-model's REVISE explicitly overrides both the carried fault-layer fork and its own round-1 claim of a fixed operator target, replacing them with a conditional keyed to which entity's next choice moves the stakes — that conditional is the only mechanism in the minutes that can produce either ai-pressure/lab-moves' lab-centered scenario or ai-public-backlash's operator-centered scenario as a function of an observable prior state (the lab's existing exposure), rather than asserting one outcome as fixed. ai-incident-severity and ai-regulation-teeth both operate on axes (fault-finding, rule-layer codification) that the minutes treat as downstream of, or orthogonal to, that targeting question.
body.threat_live: Exposure decouples from causation: whichever entity is the visible face of the deployment absorbs blame and is compelled to act regardless of where technical fault actually lies, so a lab with no proximate deployment in the flashpoint jurisdiction becomes insulated even if its model caused the harm, while an operator or a lab with local exposure eats the consequence for a failure it may not have caused. The correlate risk: whatever concessions get extracted this way become the template regulators codify, so deployment-layer rules gain real teeth while model-layer rules (SB 53, EU GPAI Code) stay theatre unless opposition explicitly names the model layer.
body.strongest_minute: ai-incident-severity — its REVISE draws a precise, falsifiable distinction between attribution (accepting responsibility for handling) and mechanism (a named reproducible failure pattern), and predicts the two decouple in the first reversal. It's a sharp, checkable claim even though it doesn't bear on the pivot.
body.weakest_minute: ai-public-backlash — it needs not just a reversal landing on infrastructure but a specific enacted state siting law in force by a fixed near-term date, which is a much narrower and more specific compound outcome than the branch it's arguing from actually guarantees.
body.shared_assumption: ai-incident-severity, ai-regulation-teeth, lab-moves, and pressure-model (in its retained portion) all rely on 'binding public opposition severs the developer/operator fault-layer fork' without independently arguing for it — pressure-model states the mechanism, the other three just build on the conclusion. Treat this as one argument, not three or four independent confirmations.
body.smuggled_assumption: ai-public-backlash's claim requires a state-level siting restriction already 'enacted' and 'in force' by 2026-11-03 — the brief grants only that pressure operates 'without any court, agency, or state law yet requiring it' at the point of reversal; asserting a specific enacted statute on a fixed near-term date is an added premise about legislative speed, not a consequence drawn from the granted branch.
body.unresolved: Whether the first visible reversal (Stage 2's trigger event) has already occurred as of this writing, and if so which entity it named — the minutes argue the downstream target conditionally but none states the actual current exposure position of any specific named lab, so the pivot is well-defined but not yet resolved by anything in the record.
